index.title: What Always Waiting Is Worth
index.prompt: In a state an agent can wait, which pays 1 and leaves it in the same state, or go, which pays 5.6 and ends the episode. Its policy picks each action half the time, the discount is 0.9, and evaluating it gives 6.4 for waiting and 5.6 for going. How much does the value of the state rise when the agent switches to waiting at every visit?
index.answer: 4.0. Before the switch, V^π(s) averages the two actions with the policy's probabilities: 0.5(6.4) + 0.5(5.6) = 6. Always waiting earns 1 at every step forever, worth 1 + 0.9 + 0.81 + ... = 1/(1 − 0.9) = 10. The rise is 10 − 6 = 4, ten times the 0.4 that the Q table seems to promise, because Q^π(s, wait) assumes the old policy takes over again from the next step.

theory.title: The State of a Card Game

prompt.p: A betting game deals a shuffled deck of 4 red and 4 black cards face up, one card per round, until the deck is empty. Before each card is turned over, the agent bets on its color. It wins 1 for a right guess and loses 1 for a wrong one. A first design gives the agent the color of the card just dealt as its state.
Which state makes the game an MDP with the fewest possible states?

choices.text: The colors of the last two cards dealt
choices.explain: Recent history is the usual repair, but it does not work here. After red, red the deck holds 2 red cards out of 6, so the next card is red with probability 1/3. After black, black, red, red it holds 2 red cards out of 4, probability 1/2. The same state gives two different chances for the next card, so the past still matters.

choices.text: The number of red cards dealt so far
choices.explain: One red card dealt can mean 3 red cards left out of 7 (after a single red card) or 3 out of 5 (after red, black, black), so the next card is red with probability 3/7 or 3/5. The chance also depends on how many cards are left, which this state does not record.

choices.text: The counts of red and black cards dealt
choices.explain: With r red and b black cards dealt, the next card is red with probability (4 − r)/(8 − r − b), and the next state is (r + 1, b) or (r, b + 1). The best bet and its expected reward depend only on that chance, so the pair carries everything the past can say about the future. It takes 25 values, from (0, 0) to (4, 4), and no two of them can be merged, because each leaves a different deck.

choices.text: The full sequence of colors dealt so far
choices.explain: This state is Markov, since it records everything, but it is far from the smallest. Red then black and black then red leave the same deck and the same future. The sequences take 251 values against 25 pairs of counts, and a table-based agent would have to learn each future several times over.

answer.p: In general the bracket is $(3\gamma - 2)w$, so each update multiplies $w$ by $1 + 2\alpha(3\gamma - 2)$. The update at $Y$ uses a target with no estimate in it, the reward 0 at the end, and it pulls $w$ down hard. With only $X$'s transition in the buffer, nothing ever checks the estimate at $Y$ that $X$'s target relies on. Linear TD is known to converge when its updates visit the states in the proportions the agent's own policy does, and a buffer filled from the agent's recent experience stays close to those proportions.

theory.title: When to Stop Sweeping
overview: Value iteration applies the Bellman optimality operator $T$ over and over, $V_k = T V_{k-1}$, and $T$ is a $\gamma$-contraction in the sup norm. The true $V^*$ is never available while the loop runs, so programs stop when the last change is small: they return $V_k$ at the first sweep where $\delta_k = \|V_k - V_{k-1}\|_\infty$ falls below a tolerance.

prompt.p: A program uses $\gamma = 0.99$ and stops at the first sweep with $\delta_k < 0.001$. How far from $V^*$ can the table it returns be, in the sup norm, by Part 1? Give the bound to three decimal places.

answer.p: A tolerance of 0.001 promises only that the values are within 0.099, about a hundred times looser. The factor $\gamma/(1 - \gamma)$ is about the horizon, 99 here, and it grows as $\gamma$ approaches 1, just when the slow convergence tempts people to stop early.

The loop stops at the first $k$ with $0.99^{k-1} < 0.001$, that is $k - 1 > \ln 0.001 / \ln 0.99 \approx 687.3$, so $k = 689$. There $\delta_{689} = 0.99^{688} \approx 0.000993$ and

Here $V^* - V_k = \frac{0.99}{0.01}\,\delta_k$ exactly, at every $k$: the bound of Part 1 holds with equality. The error is not 0.099 only because $\delta_{689}$ landed a little below 0.001. So the factor $\gamma/(1 - \gamma)$ cannot be improved, because this one-state MDP reaches it.

prompt.p: With $\gamma = 0.99$, what is the largest tolerance for which the bound of Part 1 guarantees that the returned table is within 0.001 of $V^*$? Give it in millionths (so 0.00002 is 20).

answer.p: Part 1 guarantees an error below $\frac{\gamma}{1 - \gamma}\,\text{tol}$, and that guarantee is at most 0.001 exactly when

theory.title: Five Games, Two Estimates
overview: A short game has three positions, $X$, $Y$ and $Z$. A game that starts at $X$ moves to $Y$ or to $Z$ and then ends, and a game can also start at $Y$ or $Z$. Five recorded games, written as position, reward, position, ..., end:

setup.p: Every game ends, so there is no discounting ($\gamma = 1$), and the end has value 0. Two learners start from $V = 0$ and go over the five games again and again, adding up each pass's updates and applying them together with a small step size, until their values stop changing. One uses the TD(0) update, the other moves each state toward the return that followed it.

prompt.p: Where does the TD learner's $V(X)$ settle? Give it to three decimal places.

answer.p: The values stop changing when the updates of a pass add up to zero for every state. For TD(0) that means, for each state, the TD errors of its recorded transitions sum to zero, so

answer.tex: V(s) = \text{the average over the recorded transitions out of } s \text{ of } r + V(s') .

list: $Y$ has three transitions, rewards 4, 0 and 0, each to the end: $V(Y) = 4/3$.
$X$ has two, one to $Y$ and one to $Z$, both with reward 0:

answer.p: These are exactly the values of the MDP that the counts describe: from $X$ the game went to $Y$ half the time, and $Y$ paid 4 in one game out of three. Batch TD fits that model and solves it.

prompt.p: Where does the other learner's $V(X)$ settle?

answer.p: Here the updates of a pass add up to zero when each $V(s)$ is the average of the returns that followed $s$. Two games pass through $X$, with returns $0 + 4 = 4$ and $0 + 0 = 0$, so $V(X) = 2$.

For $Y$ and $Z$ the two learners agree, $4/3$ and $1$, because their returns are single rewards. They disagree only at $X$. The one game that went from $X$ to $Y$ happened to be the one game out of three in which $Y$ paid 4, and only this learner takes that game at face value.

prompt.p: A sixth game is recorded, $Y$, 4, end, and both learners run again on all six games. What is the TD learner's $V(X)$ now? What happens to the other learner's?

answer.p: $Y$ now has four transitions, paying 4, 0, 0 and 4, so $V(Y) = 2$. Then

The other learner's $V(X)$ stays at 2. No new game passes through $X$, and it updates $X$ only from returns that followed $X$. TD's estimate of $X$ moved because it is built from its estimate of $Y$, so everything learned about $Y$ from any game reaches $X$.

prompt.p: Which of the two estimates of $V(X)$ from the five games would you use to predict the next game that starts at $X$? Describe a way the game could work in which the other estimate is the better one.

answer.p: If what happens after $Y$ does not depend on how the game reached $Y$, which is the Markov property, then the three games seen from $Y$ all describe the game that starts at $X$ and goes to $Y$. The TD estimate uses all of them, and the Monte Carlo estimate uses only the one that came from $X$. The TD estimate is the better guess, because it rests on three games from $Y$ instead of one.

The Monte Carlo estimate is better when the Markov property fails. Suppose strong players start at $X$ and weak players start at $Y$, and position alone does not record the player. Then $Y$ pays more in games that came from $X$ than in games that started there, and games 3 and 4 say little about a game that starts at $X$. TD's estimate leans on them and is biased. Monte Carlo uses only returns that actually followed $X$, so it stays unbiased however the positions are defined, at the price of noise.

theory.title: The Max of Noisy Estimates
overview: In state $s$ an agent has four actions. Each one ends the episode with a reward of $+1$ or $-1$, with probability $1/2$ each, drawn afresh every time, so every action's true value is 0. The agent has tried each action once, and with step size 1 its table holds that single reward: each $Q(s, a)$ is $+1$ or $-1$, independently.

setup.p: One step before $s$ is a state $s_0$. There the agent can **stop**, which pays 0.5 and ends the episode, or **go**, which pays 0 and leads to $s$. The agent already has $Q(s_0, \text{stop}) = 0.5$, and $\gamma = 0.9$.

prompt.p: What is the expected value of $\max_a Q(s, a)$?

answer.p: The max is $-1$ only when all four entries are $-1$, which has probability $(1/2)^4 = 1/16$. Otherwise it is $+1$. So
although $\max_a \mathbb{E}[Q(s, a)] = 0$. Each entry is an unbiased estimate, but the max picks whichever one the noise pushed up.

prompt.p: The agent now makes one Q-learning update of $(s_0, \text{go})$ with step size 1, which sets $Q(s_0, \text{go}) = 0 + 0.9 \max_a Q(s, a)$. With what probability does it then prefer go to stop?

answer.p: Go wins when $0.9 \max_a Q(s, a) > 0.5$, which happens exactly when the max is $+1$ (then $0.9 > 0.5$), so with probability $15/16 = 0.9375$.

The true value of go is 0, below the 0.5 of stopping, so the agent picks the worse action fifteen times out of sixteen. Its expected target is $0.9 \times 0.875 = 0.7875$. The overestimate in $s$ has been passed back to $s_0$, and every state upstream that bootstraps from $s_0$ can inherit it.

prompt.p: Instead, the agent keeps two tables, $Q_A$ and $Q_B$, each filled from its own independent try of every action. It chooses $a^* = \arg\max_a Q_A(s, a)$, breaking ties at random, and updates with $Q(s_0, \text{go}) = 0.9\,Q_B(s, a^*)$. What is $\mathbb{E}[Q_B(s, a^*)]$?

answer.p: The choice $a^*$ depends only on $Q_A$, and $Q_B$ is independent of $Q_A$, so whichever action is chosen, its $Q_B$ entry is still a fresh draw of $+1$ or $-1$:
the true value. The table that picks the action is not the one that values it, so the noise that made $a^*$ look best does not carry over to its value. This is the idea of double Q-learning.

prompt.p: With the two tables of Part 3, with what probability does the agent now prefer go to stop?

answer.p: Go wins when $0.9\,Q_B(s, a^*) > 0.5$, which happens exactly when $Q_B(s, a^*) = +1$, with probability $1/2$.

The agent still picks the worse action half the time, because one try per action is very little data, but its error is no longer pushed in one direction: with $Q_B(s, a^*) = -1$ it prefers stop, by a wide margin. More tries shrink the noise around the right value, 0. With the single table of Part 2, more tries shrink the noise too, but the max of the noisy averages stays above 0 on average.

prompt.p: Prove the general pattern. Let $\mu_a$ be the true value of action $a$. Let $Q_A$ and $Q_B$ be independent estimates with $\mathbb{E}[Q_A(a)] = \mathbb{E}[Q_B(a)] = \mu_a$ for every $a$, and let $a^*$ be any action chosen from $Q_A$ alone. Show that

answer.p: For the first inequality, fix any action $b$. Since $\max_a Q_A(a) \ge Q_A(b)$ for every outcome, taking expectations gives $\mathbb{E}[\max_a Q_A(a)] \ge \mu_b$. This holds for every $b$, so it holds for the $b$ with the largest $\mu_b$.
For the second, condition on $a^*$. Because $a^*$ is a function of $Q_A$, it is independent of $Q_B$, so $\mathbb{E}[Q_B(a^*) \mid a^* = a] = \mu_a$ and
since a weighted average with weights that sum to 1 is never above its largest term. $\qquad\blacksquare$

Q-learning's target uses one table both to pick and to value, so on average it errs upward or not at all. The two-table target errs downward or not at all, and only when $Q_A$ can pick a worse action. In Part 3 every action is equally good, so it is exactly unbiased.
